title: The penance grove
hook: he visits ascetics who hope for heaven through pain, and moves on (Buddhacarita 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Chandaka, thanked and sent home with the jewels. Your line: sent home with the jewels. A new week begins inside the forest.

Some of them eat only grass and leaves, the poem says, grazing like deer. Some live on what falls from the trees. Some stand in water. Some tend sacred fires and offer into them day and night. This is the hermitage the prince walks into, his hair freshly cut, his silk traded for a plain robe. The people here have given up far more than jewels, and they come out to greet him with wonder. If anyone could teach him, it ought to be them. So he asks.
screen: `GRASS, LEAVES, WATER, FIRE.` → `THEY GREET HIM WITH WONDER.` → `SO HE ASKS.`

segments.voice: First, the question. The prince asks one of the elders plainly what all this is for: the hunger, the cold water, the hard ways of living. Second, the answer. These hardships are a kind of payment. Suffer now, and win heaven after death, or a happier life to come. Pain in this life buys pleasure in the next. Third, the prince's reply, given here in paraphrase. He honors their effort, but turns the logic over and finds a problem. If you suffer now to enjoy later, you're still chasing enjoyment; you've only moved it further off. And heaven, as they describe it, ends too, the way all merit runs out, and then the round of birth begins again. He's looking for a way out of the round, not a better seat on it. And a second problem: it's the mind that drives a person toward harm or good. Torment the body and leave the mind untamed, and you've punished the servant for what the master did. Fourth, the leaving. He stays a few nights, watching and asking, then decides to go. The ascetics are sorry to lose him and ask him to stay. One of them points him toward a teacher further on, a sage named Arada, whom the poem will reach later. The prince thanks them, and goes. He doesn't call these people fools. He calls their aim too small. They were brave and sincere, paying with pain for something that wouldn't last. He keeps the bravery and drops the bargain.
screen: `WHAT IS ALL THIS FOR?` · `PAIN NOW, HEAVEN LATER.` · `STILL CHASING PLEASURE, FURTHER OFF.` · `HE THANKS THEM, AND GOES.` · then, large: `NOT THROUGH PAIN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one hard thing you do on purpose, an alarm before dawn, a strict diet, staying late every night, saying yes when you're already tired, and ask the prince's question quietly: what am I hoping this pain will buy? Some hardships buy something real and good; some are bargains that never pay out. You don't have to decide which this is; just look at it honestly, then come back to the breath.
The penance grove. A forest hermitage where ascetics endure hardship hoping for heaven; the prince honors their effort, finds their aim too small, and moves on. Today's word.
Your line: not through pain. Whatever he's looking for, it can't be bought that way. Day seven hundred eight, done.

howItsDone: Buddhist teaching often describes the Buddha's path as a middle way between indulgence and harsh self-punishment, and monastic rules in some communities include not eating after midday and simple living, but not self-torment.

chat.meaning: Pain now to buy heaven later is still chasing enjoyment, and heaven ends. He honors their effort but calls their aim too small.
